source.title: MARM: Unlocking the Future of Recommendation Systems through Memory Augmentation and Scalable Complexity
source.authors: Xiao Lv; Jiang-Xia Cao; Shijie Guan; Xiao-You Zhou; Zhiguang Qi; Yaqiang Zang; Ming Li; Ben Wang; Kun Gai; Guo-Rui Zhou

record.tranche_reason: The paper discusses language-model scaling laws as motivation and argues they do not directly transfer to recommendation systems. Its experiments measure MARM cache scaling in recommendation models, not any of the listed language-model claim versions.
record.gate_note: The paper cites language-model scaling laws and describes why it considers them unsuitable for recommendation systems. Its own results concern recommendation-model cache size, sequence length and attention depth; those are recorded under fits_no_version, not as tests of the listed versions. Cited results from other studies are not recorded.
record.test_reason: The paper argues that language-model scaling laws do not transfer directly to recommendation models, since data and parameters are not the bottleneck there and FLOPs are. Its own results scale a new quantity, cache size C=L*n*d, against GAUC and training loss of a ranking model. That is not held-out pretraining loss against parameters, tokens or compute, so it bears on no listed version. The 'power-law trend' is a visual description with no fitted exponent. V5 could be read broadly, but its form, power law in parameters, data or compute, is not what is measured. The finding is kept under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right. The authors conclude that MARM confirms a proportional, power-law-like relationship between cache size and recommendation performance. They also conclude that caching cuts per-layer complexity from O(n^2 d) to O(n d), allowing multi-layer sequence modelling at low FLOPs. They argue that NLP scaling laws do not directly apply to recommendation systems, where FLOPs, not data or parameters, is the binding constraint.
record.recipe_differences: The study evaluates cache size, sequence length and attention depth in a recommendation system; it does not reproduce language-model pretraining-loss scaling or compute-optimal allocation experiments.
record.method_sensitivity: Recommendation performance varies with cache size, sequence length, attention depth and representation dimension; the text reports that equal sufficiently large cache sizes can give similar performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Recommendation GAUC and training loss improve with MARM cache size C, with a stated 'power-law improvement trend'. Equal sufficiently large caches give similar performance whether the size comes from depth or sequence length. At small cache, length beats depth.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In streaming recommendation ranking models, performance scales with cached attention size C=L*n*d roughly independently of how C is split, once C is large.

fits_no_version.finding: At L=0, gains from raising representation dimension d saturate at about d=128.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Representation dimension in recsys sequence modules saturates around d=128 in this setup.

fits_no_version.finding: With d=128, deeper MARM and longer sequences improve performance, even at length 6400. Table 1 GAUC rises from 0.7157 to 0.7169 to 0.7183 for L=1, 2, 4.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Cached multi-layer attention depth keeps improving recsys performance.

fits_no_version.finding: Fig 1(b): halving the streaming training data with 50% downsampling gives a continuing performance decline, and cold-start training hurts badly.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Streaming recommendation models remain data-hungry; less data lowers performance.

record.peer_reviewed: CIKM ’25, as stated in the paper’s publication information
record.problems: The paper does not evaluate language models or held-out language-model pretraining loss. The cache-scaling curves are presented as plots without tabulated point values or fitted exponents in the text. The main experiments are in a real-world recommendation setting.
record.rows_left_out: No additional rows extracted. Other comparisons in Sections 3.3 and online A/B results measure recommendation modules or business metrics rather than the listed language-model scaling claim.

untested.parts: Language-model held-out loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
Extrapolation from small fitted runs to much larger ones.
Compute-optimal split of parameters and tokens.
Effect of architecture shape at fixed parameter count. The equal-cache configurations in Fig 5(c) are recsys cache configurations, not a parameter-matched shape study.
Power law in parameters, data or compute for recommendation or other regimes. Only cache size is scaled, and no fit is given.
Downstream performance as a function of language-model scale or loss.
Dependence of exponents or allocation on fitting choices.

record.verdict_notes: The record's 'discusses'/T6 classification is accepted; T3 for V5 was considered and rejected because the scaled variable (cache size) and measure (GAUC, training loss) differ from V5's power law in parameters, data or compute, and no fit is reported. Figure 1(b)'s data-downsampling result is added to fits_no_version. Cache-size curves are figure-only, with no tabulated values or exponents.

versions.untested_parts: Held-out language-model pretraining loss versus parameters, tokens or compute.
Whether small-run language-model loss fits predict much larger runs.
Compute-optimal allocation between language-model parameters and training tokens.
Effects of language-model architecture details at fixed parameter count.
Whether the same language-model loss scaling form holds in other modalities or training regimes.
Downstream language-model task performance as a function of scale or pretraining loss.
Dependence of language-model scaling exponents or compute-optimal allocation on fitting choices and setup.

rows.subject: MARM
rows.operation_detail: Grid search over representation dimension and sequence length with MARM depth L=0.

conditions.value: representation dimension d and sequence length n

rows.value: The text says that once d reaches 128, further increases have minimal impact on performance; plotted values are figure only.
rows.note: This is a recommendation-model dimension/sequence-length sweep, not a language-model loss scaling result.

rows.subject: MARM
rows.operation_detail: Sweep of attention depth L and sequence length n with dimension fixed at d=128.

conditions.value: depth L and sequence length n

rows.value: The text reports a significant positive correlation between increasing depth and sequence length and performance; increasing depth still notably improves performance when sequence length reaches 6400. Plotted values are figure only.
rows.note: The reported trend is for recommendation performance under MARM, not held-out language-model loss.

rows.subject: MARM
rows.operation_detail: Compared recommendation performance across cache sizes and configurations.

conditions.value: different depth and sequence-length settings at the same cache size

rows.value: The text reports a noticeable power-law improvement trend as cache size increases, and says configurations with sufficiently large equal cache sizes show similar performance; plotted values are figure only.
rows.note: This is the paper's cache-size scaling result for recommendation performance, not a test of any listed language-model version.
